title: Keep a Moon diary: draw the Moon for a month
description: Same time, same spot, one small drawing a night. In four weeks your notebook holds the whole lunar cycle — crescent, half, gibbous, full and back again — recorded by the oldest method there is: looking.

body.heading: The nightly ritual
paragraphs: Pick a time you can keep — just after dinner works — and a spot you can return to, even if it is one window. Each clear night, draw a circle the size of a coin and shade in the dark part of the Moon exactly as you see it, then write the date and one line: where the Moon sat, and how high.

The Moon's phases are the changing shapes of its sunlit half as seen from Earth: we always see the same face, but sunlight strikes it from a slowly changing angle through the month, so the lit part we can see grows (waxes) and shrinks (wanes). Your drawings catch that geometry in the act.

body.heading: What a month of drawings teaches
paragraphs: Within a week you will notice the lit edge flips its story: a waxing Moon is lit on the side facing the evening Sun, and each night the light eats further across the disc until full Moon rises at sunset, round and complete. Then the dark begins its own advance, and the cycle closes in about 29 and a half days — the original month, still written in the sky.

Cloudy nights are data too: mark them with a cloud symbol and keep the chain unbroken. At the month's end, lay the pages in order and flip them like a cartoon — your own Moon, waxing and waning, drawn by hand.

takeaway: Draw the Moon at the same time each night for a month and your notebook records the full 29-and-a-half-day cycle of phases — no equipment but eyes and a pencil.
materials: A notebook or a month of dated paper pages
A pencil (soft pencils shade the dark side best)
A fixed viewing spot — a window or garden corner
A torch with a red filter or cover if you want to keep your night vision (optional)
supervision: No special supervision is needed for adults and older children; younger children should be accompanied outdoors after dark by an adult.
safetyNotes: Stay in your own garden or at your own window after dark — do not wander to unfamiliar places at night for a better view.
Never look at the Sun through any optical aid while setting up, and take care on wet or uneven ground in the dark.
